This page covers U.S. O*NET / SOC 49-9071.00, Maintenance and Repair Workers, General, whose fixed-index Chinese name denotes general maintenance and repair workers. Common recruitment and industry titles include maintenance worker, maintenance technician, facilities technician, equipment repair worker, property maintenance worker, maintenance technologist, and mechanical repair technician. The official scope is to use skills from two or more maintenance or craft occupations to keep machinery, mechanical equipment, or building structures in repair. Duties may involve pipe fitting, HVAC maintenance, insulation, welding, machining, carpentry, electrical or mechanical repair, installing, aligning, and balancing new equipment, and repairing buildings, floors, or stairs. Core tasks include routine maintenance such as inspecting drives, motors, or belts, checking fluid levels, and replacing filters; inspecting, operating, or testing machinery and equipment to diagnose mechanical faults; adjusting functional parts of devices or control instruments with hand tools, levels, plumb bobs, or straightedges; repairing machinery, equipment, or structures with hammers, hoists, saws, drills, wrenches, precision measuring instruments, and electrical or electronic test equipment; ordering parts, supplies, or equipment from catalogs or suppliers as needed; and diagnosing mechanical problems and corrective action, consulting drawings, repair manuals, or parts catalogs as needed. Work features face-to-face or team discussions, 90% daily; constant contact with others, 75%; responsibility for others' health and safety, 65% very high responsibility; using hands to handle, control, or feel objects and tools, 68% continually or almost continually; outdoor work in all weather, 51% daily; hazardous-equipment exposure, 44% daily; noise exposure, 49% daily; common protective or safety equipment, 58% daily; and typical workweeks exceeding 40 hours, 62%. Major industries are real estate and rental and leasing, 20%; manufacturing, 13%; and government, 12%. BLS OOH2025 lists real estate and rental and leasing at 20%, manufacturing at 13%, and government excluding state and local education and hospitals at 12%. The remaining 55% is an arithmetic remainder, not an officially listed industry.

Work may occur in cold, heat, confined spaces, or awkward postures. Consequences of error are rated fairly serious by 27%; conflict situations occur at least yearly but not monthly for 38%. This occupation addresses safe operation of equipment and building systems. A single electric shock, pressurized disassembly, gas or refrigerant leak, missing protection during work at height or in confined spaces, inadequate lockout / tagout and isolation, or action beyond scope or authority can cause injury, equipment damage, or prolonged downtime. Most jurisdictions also impose safety, special-operation, and facility-management requirements, such as relevant qualifications, permits, and organizational authority for electrical work, welding, pressure vessels, heights, or confined spaces. If you struggle to follow standards in noisy, dirty environments with temperature changes, maintain lockout / tagout and review steps under pressure, or accept responsibility for others' safety and equipment outcomes, treat these as practical costs requiring serious consideration.

Direct answer | General maintenance and repair workers on this page correspond to U.S. SOC 49-9071.00. Work falls into several categories: (one) Preventive maintenance and inspections: perform routine tasks such as checking drives, motors, belts, and fluid levels and replacing filters, inspect equipment and building systems periodically, and record condition. (two) Fault diagnosis: inspect, operate, or test machinery and equipment to diagnose mechanical faults and determine corrective action, consulting drawings, repair manuals, or parts catalogs as needed. (three) Repair, disassembly, assembly, and adjustment: repair machinery, equipment, or structures with hammers, hoists, saws, drills, wrenches, precision measuring instruments, and electrical or electronic test equipment; adjust functional parts of devices or control instruments using hand tools, levels, plumb bobs, or straightedges. (four) Building and system maintenance: duties may involve pipe fitting, HVAC maintenance, insulation, welding, machining, carpentry, electrical or mechanical repair, and repairs to buildings, floors, or stairs. (five) Parts and outsourcing collaboration: order parts, supplies, or equipment from catalogs or suppliers as needed and check delivery, acceptance, and costs with contractors. (six) Installation and records: install, align, and balance new equipment and truthfully complete work orders, inspection records, parts records, and asset ledgers. The work cycle connects order receipt and risk confirmation—isolation and lockout / tagout—inspection or diagnosis—disassembly, replacement, and adjustment—restoration, trial operation, and acceptance—records, handover, and review. This page distinguishes this occupation from industrial machinery mechanics, HVAC and refrigeration mechanics, plumbers, electricians, stationary engineers and boiler operators, and facilities managers. General maintenance authority does not extend to construction, inspections, or statutory inspections requiring special-operation qualifications or specialist contracting.

Safety, compliance, and data boundaries | This page involves three requirement types. First, operational compliance and safety: work must remain within personal qualifications, organizational authority, and permits and follow equipment, facility, inspection, and occupational-health rules. Major repairs and changes follow graded authority and acceptance rules. Second, documentation and traceability: work orders, inspection, parts, and change records must be truthful, complete, and reviewable for safety, quality, and traceability. Do not fabricate, backdate, or sign under another person's name; make truthful supplementary entries and traceable corrections under organizational rules. Third, facility data and personal information: access-control, surveillance, resident and customer information, and equipment-operation data follow minimum necessity, permissions, and retention rules. External provision or remote access requires approval and security procedures. These are general pointers, not safety, legal, or engineering-acceptance opinions.

Records and collaboration | Truthfully record processes and outcomes under organizational work-order rules, retain originals, and make authorized supplementary entries or corrections. Do not fabricate or backdate. Report anomalies or out-of-scope conditions under site procedures and refer them to appropriate personnel. This page grants no shutdown, isolation, or repair authority.

Boundary conclusion | This page covers U.S. SOC 49-9071.00. The key distinction from adjacent roles lies in skill breadth and authority level. This occupation combines two or more maintenance or craft skills for daily maintenance and repair of machinery, equipment, and building structures, producing verifiable inspection, work-order, and acceptance records. Industrial machinery mechanics (49-9041; maintenance workers and millwrights have separate codes) focus on installation, preventive maintenance, diagnosis, and repair of industrial machinery, usually concentrating on production equipment. HVAC and refrigeration mechanics and installers (49-9021) focus on installing and repairing HVAC and refrigeration systems with specialized qualification and refrigerant-management requirements. Plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters (47-2152) focus on installing and repairing water, drainage, gas, and process piping. Electricians (47-2111) address electrical-system installation, maintenance, and code compliance. Stationary engineers and boiler operators (51-8021) address boiler and power-system operation and monitoring. Facilities managers (11-3013) address facility operations, budgets, outsourcing, and compliance. Skill breadth and authority levels differ; powers for energized, pressurized, special-operation, and statutory-inspection work cannot be carried across roles. General maintenance authority does not automatically include specialist-construction contracting or statutory-inspection qualifications.

Core principles of adjacent roles | Most roles in the same group and adjacent roles aim to keep equipment, facilities, and building systems safe and usable and make processes and outcomes traceable. They differ in work objects, skill breadth, and authority levels: production-equipment maintenance, HVAC and refrigeration systems, piping systems, electrical systems, boiler and power-operation duty, or facility operations, outsourcing, and compliance management.

This occupation's core purpose | Perform preventive maintenance, fault diagnosis, repairs, and installation on machinery, equipment, and building structures within personal qualifications, organizational authority, and safety procedures: order receipt and risk confirmation; isolation and lockout / tagout; inspection and interpretation; disassembly, replacement, and adjustment; restoration, trial operation, and acceptance; and records, handover, and tracking. Make equipment and facility availability and repair processes traceable and consistent with safety, occupational-health, and facility-management requirements.

Main objects and basis of adjacent roles | Industrial machinery mechanics follow production-equipment maintenance, mechanical-drive, hydraulic and pneumatic, alignment, and vibration-analysis requirements; HVAC and refrigeration mechanics follow system installation and repair, refrigerant, and environmental-management requirements; plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters follow water, drainage, gas, and process-piping installation, pressure-test, and code requirements; electricians follow electrical installation, repair, safety, and code requirements; stationary engineers and boiler operators follow boiler and power-system operation, monitoring, emissions, and safety requirements; facilities managers follow facility-operation, budget, outsourcing, compliance, and service-level requirements.

Main objects and basis of this occupation | Address preventive maintenance, fault diagnosis, repair, and installation of machinery, mechanical equipment, building structures, and associated systems such as electrical, piping, HVAC, doors, windows, floors, and stairs. The basis is personal qualifications and organizational authority; equipment and facility management and inspection rules; work permits, isolation, lockout / tagout, and personal-protection requirements; and occupational-health, hazardous-work, data, and information-security requirements.

General maintenance and repair workers use two or more maintenance or craft skills to maintain machinery, mechanical equipment, and building structures, delivering maintenance, parts, and work-order records. Specific work follows qualifications and authority. Insufficient evidence: this page has not obtained a wage distribution for the precise occupation in China.

Document each step under organizational equipment and safety rules for supervisor, safety, and quality review.

Main outputs of adjacent roles | Industrial machinery mechanics produce production-equipment maintenance, repair, and alignment records; HVAC and refrigeration mechanics produce system testing, repair, and environmental-compliance records; plumbers produce pipe installation, pressure-test, and clearing records; electricians produce distribution, wiring, and control-circuit installation, repair, and test records; stationary engineers and boiler operators produce operating-parameter, blowdown, and shift-handover records; facilities managers produce outsourcing contracts, service-level, budget, and compliance records.

Main outputs of this occupation | Verifiable inspection and preventive-maintenance records; work orders recording symptoms, locations, checking steps, interpretations, replacements or adjustments, parts, and acceptance criteria; isolation, lockout / tagout, and work-permit records; trial-operation, acceptance, and reinspection records; parts, outsourcing, and cost-change records; and equipment and asset-ledger updates and recurrence-tracking records.

Responsibility in adjacent roles | Responsibilities in the same group and adjacent roles are usually defined by the organization, personal qualifications, delegated authority, and safety procedures and generally concern equipment and facility users, coworkers, organizations, and public safety.

Responsibility in this occupation | This occupation is responsible for personally completed checks, interpretation, disassembly, replacement, adjustment, trial operation, acceptance, and records and for procedural isolation, lockout / tagout, protection, and permits. Appropriately qualified personnel, contractors, and safety and equipment-management departments decide under organizational rules on special operations such as energized, pressurized, high-place, confined-space, and hot work; construction, statutory inspections, and equipment alterations beyond personal qualifications or authority; and major equipment accidents, injuries, and facility-data leaks. This occupation does not replace their decisions.

Authority and approval in adjacent roles | Authority in the same group and adjacent roles comes from personal qualifications, organizational delegation, and safety procedures. It generally does not include independently deciding on work, construction, or inspections beyond qualifications or authority. Special operations, statutory inspections, equipment alterations, and external data connections should be referred to appropriately qualified people or organizations.

Authority and approval in this occupation | Inspections, diagnosis, disassembly, replacement, adjustment, trial operation, and acceptance must remain within personal qualifications, organizational authority, and work permits. Energized, pressurized, high-place, confined-space, and hot work; equipment alterations, structural changes, and statutory inspections; outsourcing contracts, acceptance, and external data connections require approval from appropriately qualified people or organizations or referral under organizational rules. Do not work without required certificates, exceed authority, or make unauthorized changes.

Limits on conclusions in adjacent roles | Conclusions in the same group and adjacent roles are generally limited to the equipment, organization, and individual's work scope and usually do not establish equipment safety, statutory inspection findings, or engineering quality. Cross-specialty, statutory-inspection, and accident-assessment conclusions have scope limits.

Limits on conclusions in this occupation | Repair conclusions state only verifiable symptoms, parameters, disassembly, replacements, and trial-operation facts, distinguishing resolved issues, observation needs, and specialist work. Do not issue unauthorized judgments or commitments beyond qualifications or authority, such as special-operation compliance, statutory inspection, structural safety, or engineering acceptance. Electrical shock, leaks, structural anomalies, recurrence, and suspected accidents require shutdown and escalation or referral. Descriptions must withstand review by supervisors, safety, quality, contractors, and regulators.

Checks before joining | Use the following six items one by one before applying or joining to avoid inferring actual duties and authority from titles or promotional wording. Base findings on written recruitment information, employment contracts, job descriptions, qualifications, authorization documents, and safety rules, and continue confirming after joining. This page lists checking directions only, not any organization's formal requirements. Special note: this occupation involves energized, pressurized, high-place, confined-space, and hot work. Some focus on property and building facilities, some on industrial equipment, some on a single HVAC, electrical, or piping system, and some on duty coverage and inspections. For industrial and trading enterprises' confined spaces, check approval, training, and supervision under Ministry Order 13; this is not a universal operator certificate.

This occupation combines two or more maintenance or craft skills for daily maintenance and repair of machinery, equipment, and building structures, producing verifiable inspection, work-order, and acceptance records. Industrial machinery mechanics (49-9041; maintenance workers and millwrights have separate codes) address industrial-equipment installation, preventive maintenance, diagnosis, and repair; HVAC and refrigeration mechanics and installers (49-9021) address system installation and repair; plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters (47-2152) address water, drainage, gas, and process piping installation and repair; electricians (47-2111) address electrical installation, repair, and code compliance; stationary engineers and boiler operators (51-8021) address boiler and power-system operation and monitoring. Skill breadth and authority levels differ; powers for energized, pressurized, special-operation, and statutory-inspection work cannot be carried across roles.

Evidence note | The occupations compared below come from O*NET classifications and public materials and help distinguish adjacent work and suitability for choices. They establish no qualification, hiring, or pay conclusions or safety or engineering-acceptance opinions. Check wages and employment separately under each occupation's SOC definition. This table makes no numerical comparisons and does not use one occupation's wages as a proxy for another. Check special-operation qualifications, organizational authority, and practice scope against primary laws and competent-authority requirements in each jurisdiction.

Introduction | The comparison has four columns: career direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and which choices it better suits. General maintenance, industrial machinery, HVAC, plumbing, electrical work, and boiler operations often connect within one facility or factory, but connection does not mean interchangeability. Changing direction requires learning qualification requirements, procedures, authority scope, statutory inspections, and responsibility boundaries.

Key difference | This occupation combines two or more maintenance skills; industrial machinery, HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and boiler-operation directions have their own task emphases. Mechanical and building settings may overlap. Occupational codes do not establish uniformly broader or narrower authority; statutory qualifications and organizational permissions require item-by-item checks.

Better suited to people willing to handle different equipment and building-system problems in one facility, enjoy hands-on work, follow procedures amid noise, temperature changes, and dirt, switch between preventive maintenance and sudden faults, and accept responsibility for safety and outcomes.

Core work and outputs: perform routine maintenance and inspections, checking drives, motors or belts and fluid levels, and replacing filters; inspect, operate, or test machinery and equipment to diagnose faults; repair machinery, equipment, or structures with hand and power tools, precision instruments, and electrical or electronic test equipment; adjust functional parts of devices or control instruments. Duties may involve piping, HVAC, insulation, welding, machining, carpentry, electrical or mechanical repair, and buildings, floors, or stairs; install, align, and balance new equipment. Outputs are inspection, work-order, acceptance, and ledger records (U.S. SOC 49-9071.00).

Industrial machinery mechanics 49-9041 focus on production and processing machinery. This occupation combines two or more maintenance skills across machinery and buildings. Codes alone cannot establish skill depth, capacity responsibility, or breadth of authority.

Editorial direction suggestion: explore industrial machinery if you want deeper expertise in production and processing machinery. This occupation also covers machinery; the settings are not mutually exclusive.

Core work and outputs: install and adjust industrial machinery and equipment, perform preventive maintenance and condition monitoring, diagnose mechanical and hydraulic or pneumatic faults, repair or replace components, and align, balance, and trial-run equipment. Outputs are equipment-maintenance, repair, alignment, and condition records.
Industrial Machinery Mechanics and Maintenance Workers and Millwrights (49-9041)

Key difference: HVAC and refrigeration mechanics and installers address system testing, charging, repair, and commissioning, usually requiring refrigerant-management, environmental, and specialist certifications and involving electrical, duct, and control systems. This occupation may perform routine HVAC maintenance such as filters, belts, and cleaning, while refrigerant circuits, charging, pressure, and specialized compliance work usually require appropriately qualified personnel.

Better suited to people who want HVAC and refrigeration installation, commissioning, and troubleshooting and accept specialist certification and environmental-compliance requirements; this occupation emphasizes routine maintenance across systems.

Core work and outputs: install and test HVAC and refrigeration equipment, repair fans, compressors, heat exchangers, and control circuits, evacuate and charge refrigerants and commission systems, and address air-quality and energy-efficiency issues. Outputs are system testing, repair, commissioning, and environmental-compliance records.
Heating, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration Mechanics and Installers (49-9021)

Key difference: plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters address prefabrication, installation, pressure testing, and clearing of water, drainage, gas, and process piping, including materials, welding, sealing, pressure tests, and code compliance. This occupation's piping duties generally concern routine repair, installation, and replacement. Gas, pressure piping, concealed works, and statutory requirements need appropriately qualified personnel.

Better suited to people who want pipe-system installation, pressure testing, and clearing and accept gas, pressure, and code requirements; this occupation emphasizes routine maintenance and repair across systems.

Core work and outputs: prefabricate and install water, drainage, gas, and process piping from drawings; connect, seal, support, and insulate it; perform pressure tests, flushing, and clearing; and troubleshoot leaks and blockages. Outputs are pipe-installation, pressure-test, and clearing records.
Plumbers, Pipefitters, and Steamfitters (47-2152)

Key difference: electricians install, repair, and test electrical distribution, wiring, and control circuits under electrical safety, codes, permits, power-supply, and inspection requirements. This occupation may perform routine electrical maintenance such as replacing fixtures, switches, and simple wiring and testing motors, while energized work, distribution alterations, code compliance, and inspections require qualified electricians.

entries.answer: General maintenance and repair workers on this page correspond to U.S. SOC 49-9071.00: use skills from two or more maintenance or craft occupations to keep machinery, mechanical equipment, or building structures in repair. Duties may involve pipe fitting, HVAC maintenance, insulation, welding, machining, carpentry, electrical or mechanical repair, installing, aligning, and balancing new equipment, and repairing buildings, floors, or stairs. Core work includes routine maintenance such as inspecting drives, motors or belts, fluid levels, and filters; inspecting, operating, or testing machinery and equipment to diagnose faults; adjusting functional parts of devices or control instruments; repairing machinery, equipment, or structures with tools, precision instruments, and electrical or electronic test equipment; ordering parts, supplies, or equipment as needed; and diagnosing mechanical problems and corrective action using drawings, manuals, and parts catalogs. Common employers include real estate and rental and leasing, manufacturing, government, accommodation and food services, educational services, and other industries. This page uses U.S. occupational-classification definitions.
entries.question: What exactly does this occupation do?

entries.answer: The key distinction lies in skill breadth and authority level. This occupation combines two or more maintenance or craft skills for daily maintenance and repair of machinery, equipment, and building structures, producing verifiable inspection, work-order, and acceptance records. Industrial machinery mechanics (49-9041; maintenance workers and millwrights have separate codes) address industrial-equipment installation, preventive maintenance, diagnosis, and repair; HVAC and refrigeration mechanics and installers (49-9021) address system installation and repair and refrigerant management; plumbers, pipefitters, and steamfitters (47-2152) address water, drainage, gas, and process-piping installation and repair; electricians (47-2111) address electrical installation, repair, and code compliance; stationary engineers and boiler operators (51-8021) address boiler and power-system operation and monitoring; facilities managers (11-3013) address facility operations, budgets, outsourcing, and compliance. Different skill breadth and authority levels mean energized, pressurized, special-operation, and statutory-inspection powers cannot be carried across roles.

subject.name: General Maintenance and Repair Workers
subject.summary: General maintenance and repair workers correspond to U.S. O*NET / SOC 49-9071.00, Maintenance and Repair Workers, General: use skills from two or more maintenance or craft occupations to keep machines, mechanical equipment, or building structures in repair. Duties may involve pipe fitting, HVAC maintenance, insulation, welding, machining, carpentry, electrical or mechanical equipment repair, installing, aligning, and balancing new equipment, and repairing buildings, floors, or stairs. Core work includes routine maintenance such as inspecting drives, motors, or belts, checking fluid levels, and replacing filters; inspecting, operating, or testing machinery and equipment to diagnose mechanical faults; adjusting functional parts of devices or control instruments with hand tools, levels, plumb bobs, or straightedges; repairing machinery, equipment, or structures with hammers, hoists, saws, drills, wrenches, precision measuring instruments, and electrical or electronic test equipment; ordering parts, supplies, or equipment from catalogs or suppliers as needed; diagnosing mechanical problems and determining corrective action, consulting drawings, repair manuals, or parts catalogs when needed; and installing, aligning, and balancing new equipment. Official scope: Perform work involving the skills of two or more maintenance or craft occupations to keep machines, mechanical equipment, or the structure of a building in repair. Duties may involve pipe fitting; HVAC maintenance; insulating; welding; machining; carpentry; repairing electrical or mechanical equipment; installing, aligning, and balancing new equipment; and repairing buildings, floors, or stairs.
